newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch share market bull run seen unbroken- for now.
newsitem.headline: Dutch share market bull run seen unbroken- for now.

text.p: The Dutch share market is not staring at the end of its spectacular two-year bull run despite a knee-jerk sell off and recovery following big declines last Friday on Wall Street, analysts said on Monday.
But, while some see a return to the all-time highs set at the beginning of August, progress could be slow and the charging gains seen over the summer could be a thing of the past.
The AEX index of 25 leading Dutch shares dropped heavily on Friday and plunged again on Monday morning, only to attract buying on a feeling that selling had been overdone.
The index dropped almost 20 points in early business on Monday to touch a session low of 875.77, a loss of more than 13 percent from the all time high of 1,011.62 points on August 7.
By early afternoon it had bounced to stand over 14 points up on the day at about 908, fuelled by anticipation that Wall Street might recover some of the three percent lost on Friday.

"We think it will be temporary, maybe a little bit longer than some people might think, but we don't think it's the end of the bull run," said Peter Wind, equities strategist at ING in Amsterdam. "It's simply a correction with the trigger coming from the United States," he said.

Analysts said Dutch economic and corporate fundamentals remained strong with few worries about inflation and interest rates on the horizon, and the expectation that companies would continue showing strong profit growth.
"We have companies earning a lot of money, we have an economic situation where we don't need higher bond yields, so you have got to be in the stock market," said Wind.

"Long term interest rates won't go up very far, simply because internationally we have a very competitive situation. We can have some economic growth without inflation. Inflation prospects aren't that scary, it's as simple as that," he added.
Bryan Allworthy, European equities strategist at Merrill Lynch in London, said holiday-thinned markets could be adding to volatility for Dutch shares.

"It's not the beginning of the end this time round. You very rarely get long-term changes in market direction in summer periods. It's basically a function of markets being relatively thin, fewer people on the ground so there's a bit more volatility at this time of the year," said Allworthy.
Analysts said events on Wall Street last Friday, partly triggered by a warning on earnings from Gillette Co, showed how much investors were focusing on company results.

"What is driving equity markets in America and to an increasing extent in Europe is corporate earnings. You need to be looking for a corporate earnings accident in America to start to call an end to the bull market run there," said Allworthy.

Analysts said attitudes of institutional and private investors were likely to remain unshaken after recent events, with institutions happy to buy dips and fill gaps in portfolios left in the spectacular run which has seen the AEX explode from 485 points since the end of 1995.
And retail buyers, who have chased stocks up from 648 since the end of 1996 have yet to be burned by a market collapse.

"They're what you might call the 'no fear brigade'. They haven't experienced a proper stock market cycle. It's always been right for them to buy dips because you can make 10-15 percent quite quickly afterwards," said Allworthy.

"One of these days they're going to buy that dip and it's going be like catching falling knives. You need a change in the retail investment psychology before you can really call the bear market," he added.
"Now isn't the time. A more appropriate time may be later on in the year when you stand a better chance of the U.S. leading that change in pyschology in the Dutch equity market."
Market watchers say the highs could be retested after a cooling off period, possibly by late September, early October.
"The 1,000 level on the AEX is not unrealistic, but it could be possible that we first touch 850 before we see 1,000 again," said Han Vermeulen, head of sales and research at Leemhuis & Van Loon.

"Why should we worry about inflation, and our interest rates? Why should we worry about third quarter company results? There's no reason. The only thing you could say is that prices have been too high and maybe we're due a correction," he said.
